reference.source: ISSVA classification / Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies
clinicalPearls: Characterised by multifocal venous malformations of the skin and gastrointestinal tract rather than a single lesion
Cutaneous lesions are soft, compressible, blue-to-purple rubbery nodules that refill after being emptied and may be tender or sweat-associated
The gastrointestinal venous malformations, most numerous in the small bowel, are the major source of morbidity through chronic occult bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia
Acute or life-threatening haemorrhage, intussusception and volvulus are recognised complications of the bowel lesions
Somatic activating variants in TEK (TIE2) are implicated, and most cases are sporadic
Lesions are venous malformations (slow-flow) in the ISSVA scheme, not tumours, and are GLUT1-negative
Localised intravascular coagulopathy with a raised D-dimer can accompany extensive venous malformations

Management is multidisciplinary and often includes sirolimus for extensive or bleeding disease, endoscopic or surgical treatment of bowel lesions, sclerotherapy for symptomatic cutaneous lesions and iron replacement
reference.pathophysiology: Blue rubber bleb naevus syndrome is a disorder of multifocal slow-flow venous malformations affecting the skin and, characteristically, the gastrointestinal tract. The malformations consist of ectatic, thin-walled venous channels lined by quiescent endothelium, and somatic activating changes in the TEK (TIE2) receptor tyrosine kinase pathway drive their formation. Because venous channels can trap and consume clotting factors, extensive lesions may produce a localised intravascular coagulopathy. Bowel lesions bleed chronically, leading to iron-deficiency anaemia, and can rarely precipitate acute haemorrhage or mechanical complications.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and iron studies to quantify chronic blood loss anaemia
Coagulation screen including D-dimer and fibrinogen for localised intravascular coagulopathy
MRI to map the extent and depth of venous malformations
Upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy and capsule endoscopy for small-bowel lesions
Faecal occult blood testing to document gastrointestinal loss
Histopathology when the diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: Acute gastrointestinal haemorrhage with haemodynamic compromise
Symptoms of intussusception or volvulus (obstruction, severe abdominal pain)
Symptomatic anaemia from ongoing occult blood loss
Evidence of consumptive or localised intravascular coagulopathy
Rapid lesion enlargement or new neurological signs suggesting central nervous system involvement
reference.prognosis: Cutaneous lesions are largely a cosmetic and comfort issue, but gastrointestinal disease often requires lifelong management of anaemia and recurrent bleeding; with iron replacement, medical therapy and targeted endoscopic or surgical treatment most patients do well, though extensive bowel involvement can be difficult to control.
pitfalls: Regarding the condition as a purely cutaneous naevus and failing to investigate the gastrointestinal tract
Missing small-bowel lesions because they lie beyond the reach of standard endoscopy
Overlooking localised intravascular coagulopathy before intervention
Attributing anaemia to another cause and delaying evaluation of occult bleeding
references: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Haemangiomas and Malformations
